children: 1156 GMT - Sterling looks vulnerable over the coming months as the U.K. is expected to face increased inflationary and fiscal pressures, RBC BlueBay Asset Management's Mark Dowding says in a note. The U.K. is exposed to greater inflationary pressure from high energy prices than its eurozone peers as it lacks gas storage facilities, Dowding says. In addition, high government borrowing costs could put further strain on public finances and hurt the economy, he says. RBC BlueBay Asset Management has an underweight position on sterling as its sees few catalysts that would support a rally in the currency over the coming months. Sterling edges up 0.1% to last trade at $1.3533. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

1152 GMT - RBC BlueBay Asset Management is skeptical that Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi would favor too strong a yen, RBC BlueBay Asset Management's fixed income CIO Mark Dowding says in a note. "Ultimately, we are skeptical that Takaichi will want too much yen strength," he says. RBC BlueBay thinks that any forthcoming change in policy is more focussed on avoiding further weakness in the yen and domestic bonds, with this having the potential to further weaken Takaichi's own position within the ruling LDP, Dowding says. The dollar is last up 0.3% at 156.20 yen, having dropped to a one-month low of 155.27 yen overnight, LSEG data show.(emese.bartha@wsj.com)

1102 GMT - The cost of euro credit default swaps is steady as market attention focuses on U.S. non-farm payrolls data due at 1230 GMT. The jobs data will indicate the state of the U.S. labor market and could provide clues on the future path of U.S. interest rates. Markets price in a 50% chance of a U.S. Federal Reserve interest-rate increase in September, LSEG data show. The iTraxx Europe Main index of euro investment-grade CDS is unchanged at 52 basis points, S&P Global Market Intelligence data show. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

1052 GMT - Thirty-year Japanese government bonds look worth buying with yields above 4%, RBC BlueBay Asset Management fixed-income CIO Mark Dowding says in a note. "We continue to highlight attractive structural value in 30-year JGBs above 4%," he says. He adds that there is "a sense that Japanese policymakers are taking the selloff in JGBs seriously, now that 10-year yields have breached 3%." Dowding also points to speculation that the Government Pension Investment Fund will substantially revise upwards its holdings of Japanese bonds within its asset allocation. The 30-year JGB yield hit a peak of 4.207% on Wednesday and last trades at 3.967%, according to LSEG. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

1028 GMT - The persistence of the energy-price shock and the eurozone economy's resilience mean the European Central Bank could be on course to raise its key rate in both September and December, BNP Paribas economists say in a note. The ECB is expected to raise rates next week and will likely also raise both its growth and inflation forecasts, supporting the case for further tightening, they say. Continued higher energy prices and a robust economy make second-round effects--of which there is so far limited evidence--more likely to materialize. Policymakers will still label risks to the inflation outlook as being skewed to the upside, the economists say. (edward.frankl@wsj.com)

1017 GMT - China's trade growth is likely to pick up modestly in August, according to Goldman Sachs in a research note. On exports, high-frequency indicators such as shipping volumes point to a mild recovery, the bank says. South Korea's reported imports from China remained solid, GS adds. "On imports, the ongoing AI capital expenditure boom should continue to support tech-related nominal imports, consistent with strong Korean exports to China in August," GS says. The bank forecasts export growth to rise to 26.0% on year in August from 23.9% in July, and for import growth to accelerate to 32.6% on year from 27.5%. (tracy.qu@wsj.com)

1009 GMT - The U.S. dollar rises while Treasury yields are steady ahead of August employment data at 1230 GMT. Yields retreated Thursday after Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller's comments pushed rate-hike expectations lower, to roughly equal odds of a rate increase and a rate hold at the Sept. 16 meeeting. Waller said he would support holding interest rates steady if next week's August inflation data backed it up. However, yields "remain at elevated levels" as an interest-rate hike is still expected before the end of the year, DHF Capital S.A's Bas Kooijman says in a note. The DXY dollar index rises 0.2% to 99.099, rebounding slightly from steep losses Thursday. The 10-year Treasury yield is steady at 4.762%, according to Tradeweb. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0959 GMT - Yields on U.K. government bonds, or gilts, decline after the Bank of England's Decision Maker Panel data showed a slowdown in U.K. businesses' price expectations. The year-ahead own-price inflation expectation was 3.8% in the three months to August, down from 3.9% in the three months to July. The DMP data is likely to lead BOE monetary policy committee members to keep interest rates on hold in the near term while they wait for additional inflation data, Pantheon Macroeconomics economists say in a note. Ten-year gilt yields fall to last trade at 5.140%, from 5.171% prior to the data release. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

0954 GMT - The 2.5% rise in German manufacturing orders in July looks goods news but only at first glance, Commerzbank economist Marco Wagner says in a note. Excluding large orders worth more than 50 million euros, orders fell on month by 1.4%. "This means the underlying trend continues to move sideways at a low level," Wagner says. Looking at the core trend that excludes the larger orders, the recovery that had begun to take hold has once again fizzled out, he says. That means a recovery in German industrial production is unlikely for the time being, especially given low water levels in the Rhine River in recent weeks and the fact that energy prices have risen again. "The German economy will therefore recover only moderately," he says. (edward.frankl@wsj.com)

0948 GMT - The Gulf's push to build new trade, energy and logistics infrastructure is likely to continue regardless of the near-term outcome of the Iran war, the Arab Gulf States Institute says. Bypassing the Strait of Hormuz is one objective, but the investment drive extends to pipelines, railways, roads, ports and new economic corridors across the region, says ASGI non-resident fellow Robert Mogielnicki. Saudi Arabia stands to benefit from a westward shift in economic activity, while the U.A.E. is developing eastern export and logistics hubs and Oman is gaining from routes that avoid regional chokepoints. (farhan.rafid@wsj.com)

0929 GMT - Gulf corporate sentiment rebounded in the second quarter despite continued disruption from the Iran war, investor-relations advisory firm Iridium Advisors says. Its GCC Earnings Call Sentiment Index rose 17% to 34.5 points across 150 calls held in July and August, the first increase since the conflict began. Management-presentation sentiment rose 15% to 45.7 points, above its long-term average, while analyst Q&A sentiment remained below its historical norm. Qatar posted the strongest country improvement at 45%, followed by Saudi Arabia at 27% and the U.A.E. at 9%. (farhan.rafid@wsj.com)

0916 GMT - Sterling could weaken in the lead-up to the budget on October 28 due to renewed political concerns, Ebury's Matthew Ryan says in a note. The government's ambitious spending plans could mean an increase in tax rates and higher debt issuance, measures which could raise U.K. political risk, Ryan says. "The political risk now seems to be grossly underappreciated ahead of the autumn budget," he says. Sterling last trades steady at $1.3525. The euro is also flat at 0.8589 pounds. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)
